title: Communication That Actually Works
excerpt: Most couples do not have a communication problem, they have a translation problem, and the difference is the whole game.
body:
I have sat across from couples who could recite the techniques. Use I statements. Reflect back what you heard. Take a timeout when it gets hot. They had read the books. They had the vocabulary. And they were one signature away from a divorce that neither of them wanted, because the techniques were sitting on top of a problem the techniques were never built to reach.

Here is what I have learned watching marriages for fifteen years, and watching my own. Most couples do not have a communication problem. They have a translation problem. Two people are speaking, and both are speaking truthfully, and neither is hearing what the other is actually saying, because they are translating the words into the language of their own fear.

A wife says, you are never home. The husband hears, you are failing as a provider, and he defends his hours. But she did not say anything about provision. She said she misses him. The sentence went out as longing and arrived as accusation, and the marriage spent the next forty minutes fighting a war that neither of them declared.

So before we talk about how to speak, we have to talk about how we listen, because the listening is where it breaks.

We do not listen to understand. We listen to defend. The moment a sentence comes at us with any edge on it, the body decides it is under threat, and the part of you that wants to be understood goes quiet while the part of you that wants to survive takes the wheel. You stop hearing your spouse. You start drafting your rebuttal. By the time they finish the sentence you are already three moves ahead, and the person in front of you has become a position to be argued instead of a soul to be received.

I know this because I do it. My wife will say something with a little heat in it, and before she has reached the period I have already decided what she meant, and I am almost always deciding she meant the worst version. That is the marriage tax on a man who is tired and a little proud. You assume the harshest reading because the harshest reading lets you stay defended.

The first discipline, then, is not a technique. It is a charity. You give your spouse the most generous reading their words will bear. When she says you are never home, you assume she means she wants you, not that she is filing a grievance. You translate up, not down. This is not naivete. It is covenant applied to a sentence. You decide in advance that the person you married is not your enemy, and you let that decision govern how you hear them when the evidence is ambiguous, because in marriage the evidence is almost always ambiguous.

The second thing is harder. You have to say the real thing.

Most marital communication fails not because people are cruel but because people are afraid, and the fear makes them indirect. We do not say I am lonely. We say you work too much. We do not say I am scared about money. We say you spent how much on what. We do not say I feel invisible to you. We pick a fight about the dishes. The dishes are never about the dishes. The dishes are the safe proxy for the dangerous truth, and the proxy is what we fight about because the truth would require us to be undefended, and undefended is the one thing we are trying not to be.

Scripture has a phrase for the alternative. Speaking the truth in love. We tend to read that as permission to be blunt as long as we are nice about it. But the Greek underneath has the sense of truthing in love, truth as a verb, a way of living and not just a way of talking. It means you do not get to use honesty as a weapon and you do not get to use love as an excuse for cowardice. The brutal man tells the truth and skips the love. The conflict-avoidant man keeps the love and skips the truth. Both are lying, just in opposite directions.

So here is a practice, and I mean a real one, not a slogan. When something is wrong between you, ask yourself before you speak, what is the actual thing under the thing I want to say. Not the dishes. The loneliness under the dishes. Then say that. It will cost you, because the actual thing is tender and the proxy is armored, and saying the tender thing means handing your spouse something they could hurt you with. That is the point. That is what it means to be naked and unashamed in a sentence and not just in a bed.

Let me steel-man the resistance, because I have heard it and I have felt it. You might say, I have tried being vulnerable and it got used against me. My spouse takes what I share and throws it back in the next argument. So I learned to stop. That is real, and I am not going to wave it away with a verse. If your honesty has been weaponized, the answer is not to keep bleeding into a wound that does not heal. The answer is to name that too. You say, I want to tell you the real thing, and the last time I did you used it against me a week later, and I need to know that will not happen before I can do it again. That is also communication. That is communication doing its hardest work, which is repairing the conditions that make communication possible.

There is also the matter of timing, which sounds trivial and is not. You cannot have the important conversation when one of you is depleted, and most couples try to have every important conversation precisely when both of them are depleted, at the end of a long day with the kids finally down and nothing left in the tank. The conversation does not fail because the issue is unsolvable. It fails because you brought a dead battery to it. A marriage needs at least one window a week that is not the leftover scraps of exhausted attention. Not a date in the entertainment sense. A window. A time when you are both awake enough to be honest and rested enough to be kind.

There is a related discipline that almost no couple practices, which is choosing the medium for the message. Some conversations should never happen by text, and yet that is where they keep happening, because the phone is always in the hand and the impulse is always fresh. Text strips out tone, and the human mind fills the missing tone with its worst guess, so a flat message gets read as cold and a brief one gets read as angry, and now two people are wounded over punctuation. The rule is simple and almost no one keeps it. If it carries weight, it waits for a face. You do not deliver the hard thing through a screen where your spouse cannot see that your eyes are soft even when your words are not. The screen is for logistics. The face is for the marriage.

And there is a particular failure I see in good, articulate people, the ones who are skilled with words, and I count myself among them, which is the temptation to use that skill to win instead of to connect. If you are better with language than your spouse, you have a kind of power, and power asks to be used. You can corner them. You can phrase the thing so cleverly that they cannot answer it, and you can mistake their silence for agreement when it is actually defeat. The articulate spouse has to lay the weapon down on purpose, has to slow down, has to ask what their less verbal partner is feeling and wait through the awkward pause while they find the words, because the goal was never to be right in front of them. The goal was to be close to them, and you cannot be close to someone you have just out-talked into a corner.

And then there is the listening that has no words in it at all. Some of the most important communication in a marriage happens when one of you simply does not leave. Your spouse is unraveling, and you do not fix it and you do not explain it and you do not improve it. You stay in the room. You put a hand on the back. Job had three friends who got everything wrong the moment they opened their mouths, and they got everything right in the seven days they sat with him and said nothing. Presence is a sentence. It says, I am not going anywhere, and that sentence carries more than any technique you will read in a book.

What actually works is not a method. It is two people who have decided that being understood matters less than understanding, who give each other the generous reading, who say the real thing even when the real thing is frightening, and who keep the door open after the worst of it. The techniques can help once that is in place. Without it they are just better tools for a war you should not be having.

The couple in my office did not need another book. They needed to put down their weapons long enough to find out that the other one had been frightened the whole time too. When they finally said the real thing, it was not articulate. It came out broken and out of order and through tears. It was the first honest conversation they had managed in two years. It did not fix everything. It opened the door. That is all communication ever does. It opens the door. You still have to walk through it, together, and keep walking through it, for as long as the marriage lasts.

title: Fighting Fair: Conflict Without Casualties
excerpt: The goal of a marital argument is not to win, and a marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing, which means the whole thing is already lost.
body:
The first lie about conflict in marriage is that good marriages do not have much of it. The couples who never fight are not the healthy ones. They are usually the ones where someone has gone underground, where peace is being purchased by one person swallowing themselves whole, and that bill always comes due, with interest, ten or fifteen years later in a counselor's office or a lawyer's. Conflict is not the enemy of a marriage. Contempt is. The two are not the same thing, and learning the difference may be the most practical skill a married person can develop.

So let me say it plainly. You are going to fight. You married a separate human being with a separate history and a separate set of wounds and a separate way of loading the dishwasher that is, you will discover, somehow morally wrong. The question is never whether you will have conflict. The question is what your conflict is for, and whether anyone walks out of it bleeding.

Here is the reframe that changes everything. The goal of a marital argument is not to win. I know that in the heat of it winning feels like the only thing that matters, and I know the rush of landing the unanswerable point, the line your spouse cannot rebut. I have felt that rush and I have hated myself an hour later, because I understood what I had actually done. A marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing, and you cannot build a covenant on a standing score. When you win the argument you lose the marriage a little, every time, until one day the losses add up to something you cannot pay.

The goal is not to win. The goal is to understand and be understood, and to come out the other side still on the same team. That is the entire art. Everything else is technique in service of that, or it is poison disguised as technique.

Now let me get specific, because vague is useless here.

There is a difference between the thing you are fighting about and the thing you are fighting for. The thing you are fighting about is the credit card statement, the in-laws, the unmade plan. The thing you are fighting for is almost always one of a small number of deep things. To feel respected. To feel chosen. To feel that you are not carrying this alone. To feel safe. The surface fights are endless and they are all reruns of the same three or four underlying ones. If you can learn to ask, in the middle of it, what am I actually fighting for here, you will sometimes discover that the credit card statement is not even the issue, that what you want is to know your spouse sees how hard you are working, and the statement was just where it surfaced.

Then there are the moves that turn a fight from a disagreement into a wound. I have a short list, and I did not invent it, much of it comes from people who have studied this far more rigorously than I have, but I have watched every item on it kill marriages, including coming close to killing things in my own.

The first is contempt. Contempt is not anger. Anger says you hurt me. Contempt says you are beneath me. It comes out in the eye roll, the mocking tone, the sentence that begins of course you would. Contempt is the single most corrosive thing you can bring into a marriage, because it does not attack a behavior, it attacks a person, and a person cannot defend against an attack on their worth except by attacking back or going cold. When you let contempt into your mouth you are no longer fighting your spouse's position. You are fighting their dignity, and dignity is the one thing covenant exists to protect.

The second is the kitchen sink, the move where the fight about tonight becomes the fight about everything, where you reach back three years and haul up every grievance you have been quietly filing. Fight the thing in front of you. One issue. If the old things keep surfacing, that is a signal that they were never actually resolved, only buried, and buried things do not stay buried, but the middle of a new fight is not the place to exhume them. Name that you need to come back to them, and come back to them when you are not on fire.

The third is the universal quantifier. You always. You never. These words are almost always false, and your spouse knows they are false, so the moment you say them you have handed them an easy out, they get to argue about the word always instead of the actual hurt, and now you are fighting about whether you are fighting fairly instead of fixing the thing. Drop the always. Say what happened this time.

The fourth, and this one is the most dangerous because it does not look like aggression, is stonewalling. Going silent. Walking out. Shutting the face down into a wall. It feels to the person doing it like self-control, like the mature alternative to blowing up. It feels to the person on the other side like abandonment, like being erased mid-sentence. Sometimes you genuinely need to stop, because you are flooded and nothing good can come out of you right now. Fine. But then you say it. You say, I am too far gone to do this well right now, I am not leaving you, I need twenty minutes, and I will come back. The difference between a wise pause and a punishing silence is whether you told your spouse you were coming back. Walking out without that sentence is not a timeout. It is a small abandonment, and the body of the person left behind knows it.

Let me steel-man the person who fights hard, because the church often shames anger and I think the church is frequently wrong about this. You might say, I come from a family that yells, that is just how we process, and my quiet spouse treats my volume like violence when it is just heat. There is something real there. Anger is not a sin. The Scriptures are full of it, including God's. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, which means the anger and the sin are separable. The issue is never that you feel it hot. The issue is what the heat does. Heat that burns the issue is fine. Heat that burns the person is not. If your volume makes your spouse go silent and small, then whatever it feels like from the inside, from the outside it is functioning as a weapon, and love requires you to know the difference and to care more about the wound than the catharsis.

And let me say something to the one who avoids. Peacekeeping is not peacemaking. The peacekeeper avoids the conflict to keep the surface calm. The peacemaker enters the conflict to make a deeper peace on the other side of it. Jesus blessed the second one and said nothing about the first. If you are keeping the peace by never saying the hard thing, you are not protecting the marriage. You are starving it, slowly, and calling the starvation kindness.

The repair is the part nobody talks about and it is the part that actually saves you. No couple fights perfectly. The healthy ones are not the ones who never cross the line. They are the ones who notice they crossed it and come back. The repair can be small. A hand on the shoulder. A softer voice. Saying I am sorry, that was beneath me, can we start over. Researchers who study this call them repair attempts and they have found that whether the attempt gets received matters more than how bad the fight got. A marriage is not measured by the absence of rupture. It is measured by the speed of repair.

The cross stands behind all of this whether we name it or not. We follow a God who absorbed the conflict instead of winning it, who took the wound rather than dealing it, who made peace by his own blood and not by anyone's defeat. Every time you choose understanding over winning, every time you take the wound instead of dealing it, you are doing something that looks, in miniature, like what was done for you. That is not a decoration on the marriage. That is the marriage doing the thing it was made to do, which is to show two people a love that does not keep score.

Fight. Fight honestly and fight about real things. Just refuse the casualties. Keep your spouse's dignity off the table no matter how hot it gets, and come back fast when you fail, because you will fail. The marriages that last are not the ones without wounds. They are the ones that learned to heal faster than they hurt.

title: Money and Marriage
excerpt: Money fights are almost never about money, they are about fear and control and worth, and a budget cannot fix a thing the budget cannot see.
body:
When couples come to me about money, they think they are coming about money. They have the numbers ready. They want me to adjudicate, to look at the spending and tell the other one they are wrong. And I have learned to set the numbers aside almost immediately, because in fifteen years of these conversations I have rarely met a money fight that was actually about money. The money is the surface. Underneath it, every time, is something older and more tender. Fear. Control. Worth. The childhood that taught you what money means and whether there will ever be enough.

You marry not just a person but a whole financial history you cannot see. One of you grew up watching the lights get shut off, and now a low balance does not register as a number, it registers as terror, the body remembering a cold house. The other grew up where money was always there and never discussed, and now the spouse's anxiety reads as irrational, controlling, no fun. Neither of you is being unreasonable given where you came from. You are being faithful to two different gods of money you were each handed before you could choose, and you brought both of those gods into the same house and the same account, and now they are at war and you think you are just disagreeing about a vacation.

So the first work is not budgeting. It is testimony. You sit down, not in a fight, and you tell each other the truth about money. What did money feel like in the house you grew up in. What were you afraid of. What did your father do with it, your mother, and what did it teach you to expect. I have watched this single conversation do more for a marriage's finances than any spreadsheet, because once a man understands that his wife's frugality is a six-year-old standing in a cold house, he stops fighting the frugality and starts comforting the child. And once she understands that his generosity is a wound too, a need to never be the man who had nothing to give, she stops calling him careless and starts seeing the fear under the open hand.

Now let me be practical, because the testimony without structure is just feelings, and money does not respond to feelings. It responds to decisions.

The single most important financial decision a married couple makes is whether the money is ours. Not legally, that is settled the day you marry. I mean in the heart, in the daily practice. There is a way of running a marriage's finances that keeps a quiet wall down the middle, your money and my money, your bills and mine, a careful ledger of who paid for what. I understand why people do it. It feels safe, especially for someone who has been financially burned before, and especially for a spouse who earns less and does not want to feel like they are asking for an allowance. But that wall is a contract wall, and a covenant has no wall. The biblical picture of marriage is one flesh, and one flesh does not run two accounts and keep score. The practice has to match the promise. If you have pledged your whole self to this person, the money is part of the self you pledged.

This cuts hard against something the culture says is just prudent. Keep your own account, just in case. Protect yourself. And I want to honor the real fear in that, because there are marriages where one spouse is genuinely reckless or genuinely abusive, and protecting yourself is wisdom and not faithlessness. I am not telling a woman married to a man who gambles the rent to hand him the keys to everything. That is not covenant, that is enabling, and they are different. But for most couples the separate-accounts instinct is not protecting against a real danger. It is keeping a door cracked toward the exit, a quiet hedge that says I have not fully bet on this. And the marriage feels that hedge even when no one names it. You cannot be all-in on a person while keeping a private bunker. The bunker is a message, and the message is, I am not sure about you.

Then there is the question of who controls the spending, and this is where most of the daily friction lives. Hear me. One person tracking the budget is fine. One person being the family's controller, having to approve the other's every purchase like a parent doling out lunch money, is not stewardship. It is a slow humiliation, and it is especially cruel when it lands on the spouse who earns less or stays home, because it tells them their work has no monetary dignity. If your spouse cannot buy a coffee or a book without filing a request, you do not have a budget. You have a hierarchy, and you have made yourself the throne. The fix is a shared plan with room in it for each person to be a free adult. You decide together what the categories are, and then within reason each of you gets to be trusted. Trust is not a reward for good behavior. It is the air a marriage breathes.

Let me name the harder cases honestly. Debt is the one that hides. A spouse opens a card, then another, covers the minimums, says nothing, and the shame of the first lie funds the second, and by the time it surfaces the betrayal is not really about the dollars, it is about the months of looking you in the eye and hiding. Financial infidelity is a real category and the church almost never talks about it, but I have watched it break trust as deeply as the other kind. If you are hiding money or hiding debt from your spouse, the dollars are not your worst problem. The hiding is. And the only way out is the way that costs you, which is to bring it into the light before you are caught, to say the number out loud, the whole number, and to let your spouse be angry without rushing them past it. The relief on the other side of confession is real, but you do not get the relief without the confession, and there is no version where you keep the secret and keep the marriage whole.

There is another fault line that runs through more marriages than couples admit, which is the gap between the earner and the one who earns less or earns nothing in dollars. In a culture that measures a person by their paycheck, the spouse who stays home with children, or whose work is unpaid, or who simply makes less, can absorb a quiet message that their contribution counts for less, and that message poisons everything. It shows up in who feels entitled to spend, in whose preferences win, in the subtle posture of the higher earner as the one doing the family a favor. This is a lie, and it is a lie the gospel directly contradicts, because the kingdom of God does not rank people by their productivity, and a marriage that secretly does is running on the world's scoreboard and not on Christ's. The woman raising five children is not a dependent. She is doing work that no salary could cover and that the family could not survive without. The husband whose business failed is not worth less than the wife whose career is climbing. If money has become the measure of worth in your house, you have a deeper problem than the budget, and it will surface as resentment long before it surfaces as a number.

And then there is the deepest thing, the thing money is always quietly asking, which is, what do we actually live for. A budget is a moral document whether you intend it to be or not. It is a record of what you worshiped, written in dollars, with no power to lie. You can tell me your priorities, and then I can read your statements, and the statements will tell me the truth. So a married couple has to decide together, not just how to spend, but what the money is for. Is it for security, for status, for the kids' every advantage, for a house that announces something to the neighbors. Or is it held a little loosely, in open hands, with generosity built into the plan before the wants get their turn. The couples I have watched stay free around money are not the ones with the most of it. They are the ones who decided early that the money serves the marriage and the mission, and not the other way around, and who put that decision into the actual numbers where it could be tested.

Jesus said more about money than about heaven or hell, and he said it because he knew the human heart attaches itself to money the way it should attach itself to God. You cannot serve both, he said, naming money almost as a rival deity, which is exactly how it functions in a marriage. So the real work is not financial. It is whether two people can hold money together with open hands, telling each other the truth, refusing the secret accounts and the secret debts and the quiet thrones, and deciding together what their one shared life is actually for. Do that, and the budget mostly takes care of itself. Skip it, and no spreadsheet will save you, because you were never fighting about money in the first place.

title: Marriage After the Kids Arrive
excerpt: The child does not threaten the marriage, but the way we organize our love around the child often does, and almost no one warns you.
body:
No one warns you that the baby can come between you. They warn you about sleep and diapers and money. They do not warn you that one night, three months in, you will look across the room at the person you married and realize you have not had a real conversation with them in weeks, that you have become two exhausted people running a small institution together, co-managers of a tiny human, and somewhere in the logistics the marriage went quiet, and you did not even notice it leave.

I have five sons. I am not writing this from theory. I am writing it from the years my wife and I nearly disappeared into the machinery of raising them, and from the slow, deliberate work of finding each other again on the other side. So let me tell you what I wish someone had told me before the first one arrived.

The arrival of a child is one of the great goods of a human life, and it is also one of the great pressures a marriage will ever face, and both of those are true at once, and the church tends to say only the first part. We sentimentalize the family in a way that quietly sacrifices the marriage to the children, as if the marriage were merely the delivery system for the kids and not a thing with its own life that the kids depend on. It is exactly backward. The marriage is not in service of the children. The children are served by the marriage. The most important thing you give your children is not your undivided attention. It is the sight of two parents who still love each other, because that is the only picture of covenant they will get up close, and they are watching it whether you mean for them to or not.

Now let me name the specific ways it goes wrong, because vague encouragement helps no one at two in the morning.

The first is that the mother and the child fuse, and the father drifts to the edge, and everyone calls it natural. In the early months there is a real biological closeness between a mother and an infant, and it is good, and it is not the problem. The problem is when it hardens into a permanent arrangement, when the mother becomes the expert and the gatekeeper of the child and the father becomes the assistant who keeps getting it wrong, until he stops trying, and she ends up doing everything and resenting him for not helping, and he ends up locked out and resenting her for the lock. Both are miserable. Both are partly right. And the way out is counterintuitive. She has to let him do it badly. He has to do it before he is asked. The father who waits to be told what to do has already made his wife the manager of two children, one of whom is him, and no woman can carry that and stay tender toward the man.

The second is that the marriage becomes a logistics meeting. Every conversation is a handoff. Who has pickup, did you call the pediatrician, the field trip form is due, we are out of the formula. This is necessary and it is not connection, and the danger is mistaking the volume of words for intimacy. You can talk all day and never once say anything that touches the other person's soul. So you have to protect a kind of talk that is not about the kids. It can be small. Ten minutes after they are down where you ask, not what is on the calendar, but how are you, actually, how is your heart in all this. If the only words between you are operational, the marriage is being run like a business, and businesses do not love each other.

The third is the death of touch that is not utilitarian. In the season of small children, two bodies get touched all day long, by people who need things from them, and by night the last thing either tired body wants is to be touched again, even in love, even by each other. I am not only talking about sex, though that goes too and we will come to it. I mean the ordinary touch that says I still see you as my spouse and not just my co-worker in this exhausting enterprise. A hand held. A long hug in the kitchen that asks for nothing. When touch becomes entirely functional, diapering and feeding and carrying, the marriage loses the language of the body, and that language is hard to get back once it goes fully silent.

Let me steel-man the parent who says, this is just the season, we will reconnect when they are older, right now the kids have to come first. I understand the instinct and there is truth in it. Seasons are real. A marriage with a newborn cannot be a marriage with a weekly date and long unhurried evenings, and pretending otherwise is its own cruelty. But here is the danger in the season that does not resolve. The kids are not going to get less demanding for eighteen years. The toddler becomes the kindergartner becomes the kid with three activities becomes the teenager whose life is a logistics nightmare of its own. If your plan is to reconnect when it calms down, you have made a plan around a calm that is not coming. The couples who get to the empty nest as strangers did not lose each other in one bad year. They lost each other one postponed conversation at a time across two decades, always meaning to reconnect later, until later arrived and there was no one across the table they recognized.

So the work is not to wait out the season. The work is to keep the marriage barely, stubbornly alive inside the season, on whatever small budget the season allows. Not the grand romance you had before. A flame kept lit on almost nothing, which is its own discipline and arguably a deeper one. Twenty minutes. A walk around the block while a neighbor watches the kids. A standing time, even fifteen minutes, that is fiercely guarded. The size of it matters less than the fact of it, the message it sends to both of you that the marriage is still a real thing and not just the foundation the family was poured on top of.

There is also the matter of division, which sounds like a chore chart and is actually a question about respect. When the children come, the sheer volume of labor in a home multiplies overnight, and how that labor gets divided becomes one of the great quiet battlegrounds of a marriage. The danger is not unfairness so much as invisibility. One spouse carries a hundred small things that never get seen, the doctor appointments tracked in their head, the shoes that got bought before the feet outgrew them, the gift for the birthday party remembered on a Tuesday, and the other spouse, genuinely unaware, thinks things are running smoothly because they cannot see the labor that keeps them running. The resentment that builds is not really about the dishes again. It is about being unseen, about doing the work of holding a family together and having no one notice it was held. So the practice here is not a perfectly equal split, which does not exist and which keeping score over will wreck you. The practice is seeing. The spouse carrying the invisible load needs it named out loud, needs to hear their partner say, I see what you are carrying, and I am not going to pretend it carries itself. That sentence does more than another load of laundry, because the loneliness was always the real wound.

There is also a spiritual thing happening here that is worth naming. Children expose you. The selfishness you could hide in a marriage of two adults gets dragged into the open by a creature who needs everything and gives nothing back for years. You discover how much of your patience was situational, how much of your kindness depended on getting enough sleep, how thin the love runs when it is tested past the point of reciprocity. This is grace, though it does not feel like it. The exposure is the beginning of being changed. You cannot repent of a sin you cannot see, and parenting makes a hundred sins visible that marriage alone never reached. The couple who lets this work on them, who confesses to each other when the exhaustion turns them mean, who forgives the short temper of a depleted spouse, comes out not just as parents but as people who have been sanded down to something humbler and more durable.

And the children are watching all of it. They will not remember the spotless house or the perfect birthday parties. They will carry, in their bodies, the answer to one question they never asked out loud, which is whether love lasts. They learn it from you, in the kitchen, in the way you speak to each other when you are tired, in whether their father turns toward their mother or away. You are writing their first theology of love before they can read, and you are writing it not with your words but with your marriage. Keep the marriage alive, not at the expense of the children, but as the deepest gift you will ever give them, the proof in front of their eyes that two people can stay, and keep choosing each other, all the way through the years that try the hardest to pull them apart.

title: Intimacy in a Christian Marriage
excerpt: The church handed most of us a theology of sex made of two words, do not and do, and then expected a married couple to build a life on the wreckage of that silence.
body:
The church taught a generation that sex was dangerous, then handed them a ring and expected the danger to evaporate overnight. We spent eighteen years telling young people that desire was a threat to be managed and the body a temptation to be guarded, and then on the wedding night we expected all of that to flip, instantly, into freedom and delight, as if a wedding could undo two decades of formation. It does not work that way. The shame does not come off with the dress. And so a great many Christian marriages carry a wound into the bedroom that no one prepared them for and that almost no one will talk about, because the same silence that caused it makes it impossible to name.

So let me try to name it, with honesty and with taste, because this matters more than the church's awkwardness allows it to admit.

Start with the theology, because the theology is the problem and the theology is the cure. The Scriptures are not embarrassed about the body. God made it, called it good, and built desire into it before there was any sin to manage. The Song of Solomon sits in the middle of the Bible, an unashamed celebration of two lovers wanting each other, and the church has spent centuries trying to make it about something else because we could not believe God meant it about the thing it is plainly about. He did. The one-flesh union is not a concession to weakness. It is part of the original design, a good thing God made for joy and for closeness and for the deep knowing that the Hebrew language captures when it says a man knew his wife, using the same verb it uses for knowing God. Sex is a way of knowing. That is the high view, and the church mostly failed to teach it, preferring the low view that treats the marriage bed as merely the licensed version of a previously forbidden act.

Now the practical truth that follows. Physical closeness in a marriage is a language, and like any language it can fall silent, and when it falls silent the marriage gets cold in a way that touches everything else. But here is what I have learned watching couples, and it cuts against the cliche. The bedroom is rarely where the problem starts. It is where the problem shows up. A couple's physical closeness is a thermometer, not a thermostat. It reads the temperature of the whole relationship. When a wife does not want to be touched, it is very often not about the touch, it is about the fact that she was dismissed at dinner, or that she has felt like staff and not like a wife for three weeks, and the body will not give what the heart has not been given. When a husband withdraws, it is often not disinterest but discouragement, the quiet ache of a man who has felt rejected enough times that he stops reaching to avoid the rejection. The physical distance is almost always reporting an emotional distance. Treat the symptom and you fix nothing. Tend the marriage and the body usually follows.

Let me be specific about the wounds, because generalities are useless here.

There is the couple where one wants closeness far more than the other, and the gap has become a battleground, the higher-desire spouse feeling perpetually rejected and the lower-desire spouse feeling perpetually pressured, each reading the other as the problem. This is one of the most common and most painful patterns in a marriage and it almost never resolves through demand or guilt. It resolves, when it resolves, through the higher-desire spouse learning that pressure kills the very thing they want, and the lower-desire spouse learning that their spouse's reaching is not only appetite, it is a need to be wanted back, and a long pattern of refusal lands as a verdict on their worth. Both have to move toward the other. The verse most weaponized in this conversation, the one about not depriving each other, was never meant as a club for the higher-desire spouse to swing. Read it again. It commands mutual self-giving, each one tending to the other, which is the opposite of one spouse owing the other a service on demand. It is two people refusing to use the body as a weapon, whether the weapon is pressure or withholding.

There is the couple carrying the wreckage of pornography, where one of them brought a privately formed appetite into a shared bed and the other now feels measured against images, never enough, competing with a fantasy that asks nothing and gives nothing real. I will not soften this. It is a betrayal of the one-flesh promise even when no other person was ever touched, because it trains the heart to want the unreal and to find the real lacking, and it leaves a spouse feeling like a disappointment in their own marriage. The road back is long and it is not walked by willpower alone. It is walked through confession, through real accountability with other people, and through the slow relearning that the actual person in the bed, with her actual body and her actual history, is the gift, and the fantasy was the counterfeit. The good news the church forgets to preach here is that this can heal. I have watched it heal. But not in secret, and not alone.

And there is the couple where one of them carries an old wound from before the marriage, an assault, an abuse, a violation that lives in the body long after the mind has tried to move on, so that touch that should mean safety triggers an alarm that has nothing to do with the spouse and everything to do with what was done to them. If that is your marriage, hear me carefully. This is not a spiritual failure and it is not yours to fix by trying harder. It is a wound that needs a real healer, often a trained one, and the most loving thing the other spouse can do is to become the safest possible presence, patient past the point of patience, never making the wounded one feel like a project or a disappointment. Covenant love here looks like a man who decides his wife's healing matters more than his own appetite, and who proves it over years, not weeks.

Let me steel-man the couple who would say, we just are not very physical and we are fine, do not make us feel broken for it. Fair. There are seasons, illness, age, exhaustion, where the body is simply not the marriage's main language, and a couple can be deeply close through other doors. I am not handing anyone a quota. The danger is only this. Sometimes we call it fine when it is actually surrender, when two people quietly agreed to stop trying because trying kept ending in hurt, and the peace is the peace of a thing abandoned, not a thing at rest. Only you know which one you are. But ask honestly, because the comfortable story is the one that lets us avoid the conversation that might actually reopen the door.

Under all of it is a truth the world cannot teach because the world does not have it. The deepest intimacy is not technique and it is not frequency. It is being fully known and not abandoned. Adam and Eve were naked and unashamed, and the nakedness was not only of the body, it was of the whole self, two people utterly seen and utterly safe, and that is the thing the act was always pointing at. Most of us are terrified of being fully seen because we believe that if our spouse really knew us they would leave. The miracle of a covenant marriage is that you get to test that fear against a love that does not leave, to be known all the way down, the body and the history and the shame and the failure, and to discover that you are still held. That is what the bedroom is supposed to rehearse, and it is why the world's version, all appetite and no covenant, leaves people emptier the more they have. They got the nakedness without the not-abandoned, and the nakedness without the safety is just exposure.

The church owes married people a better word than do not and do. It owes them this. Your desire for each other is good, your body is not your enemy, the wounds you carry can heal, and the closeness you are after is not finally about the body at all. It is about being fully known by one person who has promised never to leave, and learning, in a marriage bed and everywhere else, to stop hiding from the one you are safest with. Most couples are not under-skilled. They are under-known. Close that distance, and the rest has somewhere to grow.

title: Forgiveness and Repair
excerpt: Forgiveness cancels the debt, but it does not rebuild the house, and a marriage needs both, which is why so many couples forgive and stay broken anyway.
body:
Forgiveness is not the same as repair, and the failure to know the difference has left more marriages stranded than almost anything I can name. A couple forgives. They mean it. The offended spouse genuinely releases the offense, lets go of the right to punish, refuses the cold revenge of bringing it up forever. And then six months later they are bewildered, because they forgave and the marriage is still broken, still distant, still not what it was. They thought forgiveness was the whole repair. It was only the first step of it. Forgiveness cancels the debt. It does not rebuild the house. And a marriage that has been damaged needs both, and the second one is the longer work and almost no one talks about it.

So let me draw the distinction carefully, because the practical life of a marriage depends on getting it right.

Forgiveness is something you can do alone. It does not require the other person's cooperation, or even their repentance, though their repentance makes it far easier. You can forgive a spouse who is not sorry, the way Christ forgave from the cross people who were not asking for it. Forgiveness is the decision to stop holding the offense against the person, to release them from the debt, to refuse to make them pay it back through your coldness or your punishment or your quiet permanent withdrawal. It is between you and God before it is ever between you and your spouse. And it is commanded, not because the offense did not matter, but because you have been forgiven a debt next to which every debt anyone owes you is pocket change. The unforgiving servant in the parable was not wrong that he was owed. He was wrong that his being owed mattered more than his having been forgiven.

But repair is a different thing, and repair takes two. Repair is the rebuilding of trust, the relearning of safety, the slow reconstruction of a thing that was broken. And trust, unlike forgiveness, is not freely given. It is earned back. This is where so much bad teaching does real damage, because it tells the wounded spouse that if they have truly forgiven they should trust again immediately, as though continuing to be careful were a failure of faith. It is not. Forgiveness is free. Trust is rebuilt. To forgive your spouse is to release the debt. To trust your spouse again is to watch them prove, over time, that the thing that broke will not break again. You can do the first today. The second one your spouse has to help you with, and it takes as long as it takes.

Now let me get concrete about the repair, because this is where I can actually help.

The first thing repair requires from the one who did the wounding is a real confession, and most confessions are not real. The fake confession protects the one confessing. I am sorry you feel that way. I am sorry if I hurt you. I am sorry, but you have to understand my side. Every one of those is a defense wearing the costume of an apology, and the wounded spouse can feel the costume even when they cannot name it, which is why the apology lands flat and the fight reignites. A real confession names the specific thing, owns it without an excuse attached, and does not demand to be forgiven on a schedule. It says, I did this thing, it was wrong, I see what it cost you, and I am not going to rush you through your hurt to get my relief. The willingness to sit in your spouse's pain without defending yourself is most of what makes an apology believable. The man who cannot stand his wife's anger at what he did, who keeps trying to manage her back to calm, is still protecting himself. Real repentance can bear the weight of the other person's pain.

The second thing repair requires is changed behavior, and changed behavior is the only thing that actually rebuilds trust, because trust is a prediction. To trust someone is to predict their future conduct based on a pattern. When the pattern breaks, the prediction breaks, and you cannot talk your way back into being predictable. You can only act your way back, over enough time that a new pattern forms. This is why words are nearly worthless in the early repair of a serious breach and why the wounded spouse who keeps asking for more reassurance is not being difficult, they are waiting for the only thing that works, which is time plus consistency. The spouse who did the wounding has to make peace with this. You do not get to decide when you are trusted again. The wound decides, on its own clock, and your job is to keep proving yourself faithful through the long uncertain middle without resenting the person for not getting there faster.

The third thing, and this one is for the wounded spouse, is that at some point forgiveness has to stop being re-litigated. There is a difference between rebuilding trust, which is legitimate and slow, and punishing, which dresses itself up as caution but is actually revenge on the installment plan. If you have forgiven, you have given up the right to use the offense as a weapon in every future conflict, to reach back for it whenever you want the upper hand, to make your spouse pay for it again and again under the banner of not being over it yet. Being careful is not the same as keeping the wound open on purpose because the open wound gives you power. Only you know which one you are doing, but you do know, if you are honest, and the marriage cannot heal while the offense is kept on a shelf within reach, loaded, just in case.

Let me steel-man the hardest case, because I do not want to be glib about the deep betrayals. Some wounds are not a harsh word or a thoughtless season. Some are an affair, an addiction hidden for years, a betrayal that broke something foundational. And in those cases the talk of repair can sound obscene, like asking the betrayed to do all the work of healing a wound they did not inflict. So let me be clear. The burden of repair falls heaviest on the one who did the breaking, not the one who was broken. The betrayer does not get to set the timeline, demand forgiveness, or treat the marriage's survival as a foregone conclusion they are owed. And forgiveness, even in these cases, does not always mean the marriage continues. You can forgive and still conclude that the trust cannot be rebuilt, or should not be, where the danger is real. Forgiveness is always required of the Christian. Reconciliation is not always wise, and sometimes it is not even safe, and the church has done real harm by collapsing the two and sending people back into danger in the name of faith. Forgive, always. Reconcile, when it is true and safe to do so. Those are different decisions and you are allowed to make them separately.

Under all of it is the only model that finally works, which is the cross, where forgiveness and repair are both on full display. God forgave freely, before we asked, while we were still enemies, paying the debt himself rather than making us pay it. That is the forgiveness. But he did not stop at canceling the debt. He went on to rebuild the relationship, to reconcile, to make a new covenant and dwell with his people again, which is the repair. The gospel is both, the free release and the costly rebuilding, and a Christian marriage gets to participate in both. You forgive the way you were forgiven, freely and without making your spouse earn it. And then you rebuild the way God rebuilds, patiently, over time, through proven faithfulness, until the house that was broken is standing again, not as it was, but stronger in the broken places, the way bone heals thicker where it cracked.

Most marriages do not fail because the wound was too deep to forgive. They fail because the couple forgave and thought that was the end of it, and then could not understand why they were still cold and still distant and still alone in the same house. Forgiveness opened the door. Repair was the long walk through it, and the walk is the part that asks for everything, and the part that, if you take it, gives you back a marriage that knows how to break and heal, which in this life is the only kind of marriage there is.

title: Marriage Through Depression and Crisis
excerpt: When one of you goes dark, the vow stops being a feeling and becomes a structure, and the structure is the only thing that holds when the feeling is gone.
body:
There comes a season in many marriages when one of you goes dark. Not difficult. Dark. A depression that flattens the person you married into someone who cannot get off the couch, cannot feel the love you are offering, cannot say why, cannot promise it will lift. Or a crisis crashes in from outside, a diagnosis, a lost job that takes a man's sense of himself with it, a child in trouble, a grief that does not have an end date. And the marriage that worked when both of you were well discovers it has to learn an entirely different way to function, because one of the two people holding it up has, for now, let go of the rope.

I have walked through dark seasons in my own life and I have sat with too many couples in theirs, and I want to say some honest things, because the church often handles this terribly, reaching for a verse like a bandage over a wound that needs surgery.

First, the depressed spouse is not choosing this and cannot simply choose their way out, and a marriage that treats depression as a failure of will or faith will pour shame onto a person already drowning in it. Depression is not sadness and it is not a bad attitude and it is very often not even about anything, which is the cruelest part, because the well spouse keeps trying to fix the cause and there is no cause to fix. The illness lies to the person who has it. It tells them they are a burden, that their family would be better off without them, that they have always been like this and always will be, that the love around them is not real or is not for them. None of it is true and all of it feels truer than anything they have ever known. If you are married to someone in this, your first job is to refuse to believe the illness's account of your spouse, and to keep telling them the truth they cannot feel, knowing the words may not land, saying them anyway, because someday the fog will lift and they will need to have heard them.

Let me say the thing the church will not. Get the help. Real help. A doctor, a counselor, medication if it is called for, and I will not let anyone shame a brother or sister for taking it. The notion that a faithful Christian should be able to pray their way out of clinical depression has killed people, and I mean that literally. We do not tell the diabetic that insulin shows a lack of faith. The brain is an organ. Sometimes it gets sick. Treating it is not unbelief, it is stewardship of the body God gave you, and the spouse who gently insists on real treatment, who makes the appointment, who goes along, is doing one of the most loving things a marriage allows. Prayer and a doctor are not rivals. Take both.

Now the harder, lonelier truth, the one for the well spouse, because there is a special grief that no one warns you about, which is the grief of being married to someone who is alive but absent. You are not a widow and you are not divorced, but the person you married is somewhere you cannot reach, and the marriage gives you nothing back for a long time, and you are exhausted and you are lonely and you feel guilty for being either because they are the one who is suffering. Hear me. Your suffering is real too. Caring for a depressed or sick spouse is one of the heaviest loads a human being carries, and carrying it does not make your own depletion selfish. You cannot pour from a dry well for years and stay standing. You need your own support, your own people, your own help, and getting it is not abandonment, it is the only way you survive long enough to be there when the season turns.

This is where the vow stops being a feeling and becomes a structure, and the structure is the entire point. When we marry, we promise in sickness and in health, for better and for worse, and we say the words on the best day of our lives when the worse is unimaginable. The words are not for that day. The words are for this one. The vow is precisely the thing that holds the marriage together when the feelings that usually hold it have gone silent, and a marriage built only on feeling will not survive the season when one person cannot feel anything at all. The covenant is load-bearing. It carries the weight the emotions used to carry, and the discovery that it can, that the promise holds when nothing else does, is one of the few mercies hidden inside a dark season. You learn what your vow was actually made of, and you find out it was made of something stronger than your mood.

Let me steel-man the spouse at the edge of leaving, because I have sat with them and I will not pretend the case is weak. You might say, I did not sign up for this, the person I married is gone, it has been years, I am withering, and surely God does not require me to disappear into someone else's illness forever. I want to honor how much pain is in that, and I want to refuse the easy answer in both directions. I will not tell you that leaving is always sin, because there are situations, untreated and dangerous, abusive, where staying is not faithfulness but destruction, and you are not required to be destroyed. But I will tell you this. Depression and crisis are seasons far more often than they are life sentences, and the spouse who leaves in the dark of it frequently leaves just before the dawn they could not see coming, and carries the leaving forever. Before you decide the person is gone, make sure you fought for them the way you would want to be fought for if it were you in the dark, because someday it may be, and the way you treat your spouse in their worst season is the sermon you are preaching to yourself about what your own worst season will hold.

There is also a strange grace that the church almost never names, which is what these seasons make of the well spouse. To love someone who cannot love you back, to keep returning to a person who gives you nothing in return, to serve without reciprocity for a long time, is the closest most of us will ever come to loving the way God loves us. He loved us while we were dead, Paul says, dead, giving nothing back, unable even to reach for him. The well spouse in a dark season is being conformed to that love, ground into a shape they would never have chosen, and the love that comes out the other side is not the eager love of the wedding day, it is something deeper and more terrible and more like the real thing, a love that has been tested against an empty room and did not leave.

And to the one in the dark, if you are the one who cannot feel it, hear this. You are not a burden, whatever the illness tells you. Your worth does not run on your usefulness, and the love around you is not a debt you have failed to pay. Stay. Get the help. Let the people who love you carry you through the part where you cannot carry yourself, because that is what the carrying is for, and someday the fog will thin and you will be able to receive again what was given to you in the dark, and you will find it was real the whole time. The marriage held while you could not. That is not your failure. That is the covenant doing the exact thing it was made to do.

Weeping may last for the night, the psalm says, but joy comes in the morning. It does not say how long the night is. Some nights in a marriage are years long. The promise is not that the night is short. The promise is that there is a morning, and that the God who keeps the marriage through the dark is the same God who is bringing the dawn, even when no one in the house can see it yet.

title: Leading and Serving Each Other Spiritually
excerpt: Most marriages have no spiritual life together because both people are waiting for the other one to go first, and the waiting can outlast the marriage.
body:
Most Christian marriages have almost no spiritual life together, and almost no one will admit it. They go to church. They might pray over a meal. But the idea that a husband and wife actually walk with God side by side, pray together with any honesty, talk about their souls, lead each other toward Christ, is for most couples a quiet failure they carry privately, each one assuming everyone else has it figured out. They do not. And the reason it stays broken is almost always the same. Both people are waiting for the other one to go first, and the waiting can outlast the marriage.

I want to talk about what spiritual leadership in a marriage actually is, because the word leadership has been so badly handled in the church that for many couples it has become either a weapon or a joke, and the real thing has gotten lost between the two distortions.

The first distortion is the one that turns leadership into rank. In this version the husband leads because he is in charge, his will is the tiebreaker, his preferences carry extra weight because of his office, and the wife's job is to get in line. This reads a couple of verses about headship while skipping the sentence that defines what the head is supposed to do, which is to love as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The head, in the only definition the New Testament gives, is the one who dies first. Christ's leadership of the church is a crown of thorns and a borrowed tomb. He led by washing feet, by taking the lowest place, by laying his life down. So when a man uses headship to get his way, to win the argument, to be served, he is not exercising the leadership the Scriptures describe. He is inverting it. The biblical head is not the one who is served. He is the one who serves hardest and loses most and dies first, and any man who wants the title without that job description wants a throne the New Testament never offered him.

The second distortion is the overcorrection, where in reaction to all that abuse we throw the whole category out and pretend a marriage needs no spiritual initiative from anyone, that it will just happen by drifting, two people privately doing their own thing before God and never bringing it into the shared life. And it does not happen. A garden untended does not become a meadow. It becomes weeds. A marriage with no one taking spiritual initiative does not become spontaneously holy. It becomes two roommates who happen to attend the same church, and the shared soul of the thing slowly dies of neglect while both people congratulate themselves on not being domineering.

So let me offer what I think the real thing is, and it is not a hierarchy and it is not a vacuum. It is mutual servanthood with someone willing to go first. Paul opens the whole passage on marriage with a line we skip because it inconveniences the argument we wanted to have. Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. To one another. The mutuality is the frame around the whole picture. A Christian marriage is two people competing to out-serve each other, each trying to wash the other's feet first, and within that mutual self-giving, yes, someone often has to take initiative, to be the one who says let us actually pray, let us actually talk about our souls, let us not let this die. That initiative is not rank. It is service. It is the willingness to risk the awkwardness of going first.

Now let me be practical, because this is where couples are most stuck, and the stuckness is usually about a fear they will not say out loud.

The fear is exposure. Praying out loud with your spouse, honestly, about the real things, is one of the most vulnerable acts in a marriage, more exposing for many couples than the bedroom. To pray honestly in front of the person who knows your failures is to be seen by them and by God at the same time, to confess what you actually want and fear and have done wrong while the one you have wronged is listening. That is why couples who can argue about anything cannot pray together. It is not too holy. It is too naked. So the place to start is not a grand devotional program. It is small and it is brave. One sentence of honest prayer at the end of the day. Not performance. Not the polished prayer you would pray at church. The real one. God, I am scared about the money. God, I was short with the kids today and I hate who I was. The honesty is the whole thing, and the honesty in front of your spouse is what knits the souls together, because you cannot be that exposed before someone and stay strangers.

Then there is the matter of reading and talking. Not a seminary class at the kitchen table. Just the willingness to bring your actual inner life into the shared conversation, to say what God has been doing in you, what you are wrestling with, what the sermon stirred up, where your faith is thin right now. Most couples talk about everything except this, the logistics and the kids and the news and the in-laws, and never the one thing that is supposedly at the center of their lives. The marriage gets a body and a budget and a calendar and no soul, and then we wonder why it feels hollow. The soul of a marriage is built in these conversations, the ones about what is actually happening between each of you and God, and they do not start themselves. Someone has to be brave enough to ask the question and mean it.

Let me steel-man the wife in a marriage where the husband will not lead, because this is the most common and most painful version, and the church frequently lays the failure at her feet, telling her to wait and submit and pray him into leadership while the years pass and nothing changes. Hear me clearly. You are not required to let the marriage's spiritual life die while you wait for a man to become someone he is not yet. Mutual submission means you also get to take initiative. If you are the one who longs for the shared prayer, the honest conversation, the walk with God side by side, then lead toward it, gently and without contempt, not nagging him into shame but inviting him into something good. Many a man has been drawn into a depth he could not start himself by a wife who went first with grace. And if he still will not come, your own faithfulness is not contingent on his. You walk with God whether or not he joins you, and you keep the door open, and you refuse to let his failure determine yours. That is not rebellion against headship. That is the love that hopes all things, doing in the dark what the other one should have done in the light.

And a word to the man who knows he has abdicated, because many of us have, and I include myself. Spiritual leadership is not a personality. It is a decision, renewed daily, to take responsibility for the soul of your marriage and your home, and it does not require you to be eloquent or theologically impressive. It requires you to go first into the humbling places. To be the first to confess when you were wrong. To be the first to say let us pray, even when your voice shakes. To be the first to forgive, the first to serve, the first to kneel. The leadership the New Testament describes is not the man at the head of the table being served. It is the man on his knees with a towel, washing the feet of the people he was given to love, going lower than all of them, dying first. If you want to lead your marriage, that is the road, and it is the only road, and it is open to you tonight, in your own kitchen, with a single honest sentence said out loud to God while your spouse listens. Go first. The whole thing turns on someone being willing to go first, and it might as well be you.
